_comment: INTELLIGENCE X (intelx.io) — the SELECTOR search layer. IntelX indexes leaks, stealer logs, pastes, darknet mirrors, WHOIS snapshots and a web crawl, and it is queried by STRONG SELECTOR only (an email, a domain, a URL, an IP/CIDR, a phone number, a wallet, a MAC/UUID/IBAN/credit-card). It does not do keyword search, so 'find me the scam' is not a query it can answer — 'what else is attached to registrant@example.com' is. This file holds everything about IntelX that changes without our code changing: the API paths, the selector patterns, the bucket catalogue and how much each bucket is worth as evidence, the free-vs-paid entitlements, the spend guard, and the web-UI templates the KEYLESS path emits. Edit this file, not wp_intelx.py. Nothing here is case data — these are public product facts and generic patterns.

endpoints._comment: IntelX API paths, relative to the account's API root (https://2.intelx.io for a normal API key; a free/public key is issued against a different instance — set INTELX_BASE_URL to whatever the Developer tab shows for your account, the paths are the same). Auth is the `x-key` HTTP header on every call. The search endpoints are TWO-STEP by design: POST starts a search and returns an `id`, then you GET the result repeatedly until `status` says stop (0 = results, 1 = no more, 2 = id unknown, 3 = nothing yet, keep polling). HTTP 402 means the account is out of credits.

search_status._comment: The `status` field returned by both result endpoints. The poll loop MUST honour these: 3 means the backend is still aggregating and an empty page is NOT an empty result — treating 3 as 'nothing found' is the single easiest way to write a false negative into an assessment.

entries.0: results in this page — keep polling
entries.1: no more results — the search is complete
entries.2: search id not found (expired or terminated)
entries.3: no results YET — the backend is still aggregating, poll again

selector_types._comment: IntelX accepts STRONG selectors only; a soft/generic term is rejected outright. Each entry maps a selector class to the pattern that recognises it, whether IntelX can search it, and what it is worth as a pivot. `regex` is matched case-insensitively against the whole trimmed value. Order matters — the first match wins, so the specific patterns (email, url) come before the loose ones (domain, phone). Tune a pattern here when a real-world value is being misclassified; do not add a pattern for a SOFT term (a brand name, a person's name) — IntelX will refuse it and the run wastes a credit.

email.value: highest-yield IntelX selector — leak/stealer-log membership, pastes, and (via phonebook) the domains the address appears under

url.value: exact-URL sightings: archived copies, paste mentions, stealer-log entries naming the login page

ipv4.value: sightings of the origin IP in leaks/logs/pastes — corroborates a co-tenancy claim from an independent corpus

cidr4.value: range sweep — use only on a small operator-owned block, never on a provider /16

bitcoin.value: payout address sightings — pastes and forum posts that name the wallet, often with the campaign's own advertising copy

mac.value: device-level selector; rare in web cases, common in stealer-log work

uuid.value: SaaS tenant / project / device identifiers lifted from a page or an app

phone.value: contact-number sightings — ties a support/Zalo/WhatsApp number to leaks, pastes and other listings carrying the same number

domain.value: the workhorse — accepts a `*.example.com` wildcard, and is the only selector the PHONEBOOK endpoint turns into an inventory of every email/subdomain/URL IntelX has seen under that apex

pivot_kind_map._comment: WebPivot pivot `kind` -> the selector class above, i.e. which extracted artifacts are worth reversing on IntelX. Every key here is a kind the collector actually emits (grep `add("` in WebPivot/tools/wp_pivots.py and `"kind":` in whois_enrich.py before adding one). A kind that is absent gets NO IntelX query, which is the correct outcome for things IntelX does not index — favicon hashes, GA4 IDs, JARM, ETags. Prefix entries ending in `:` match any kind starting with that prefix; the VALUE is still classified before anything is emitted, so a mapped kind carrying an unsearchable value simply produces nothing. Do not add a kind hoping it works: a soft selector is refused by the API and still costs a search.

buckets._comment: The IntelX bucket catalogue, with what a hit in each one actually PROVES. `rank` orders them by INVESTIGATIVE VALUE (1 = read this first) and results are sorted by it, because the buckets are not interchangeable and the difference is large. THE KEY DISTINCTION — a STEALER LOG beats a BREACH DUMP, and not by a little: a breach dump is one site's user table, so a hit says only 'this address had an account somewhere, some year' — recycled, endlessly re-shared, usually years stale by the time it is public. A stealer log is a snapshot of ONE infected machine at ONE moment: the URL + username + password triple WITH its session context, plus cookies, autofill and the host's own identity. That is a different class of fact. It gives a date anchor tied to a machine, it exposes ADMIN/PANEL URLs the public site never links (feed those to the victim/access-vector layer), its credentials are comparatively fresh — and, the case-making one, OPERATORS GET INFECTED TOO: a log whose machine holds the scam infrastructure's own panel URL and credentials is direct attribution, not exposure. So rank the logs first and read them item by item; skim the breach dumps for dates only. `grade` is the evidential weight of a hit: strong = the record is about the target specifically; context = it places the target in a corpus; weak = presence tells you almost nothing on its own. `access` records which entitlement is needed to READ the item's content (metadata is usually visible to any key). Bucket names vary a little by account tier; an unknown bucket is reported ungraded and ranked last, never dropped.

leaks.logs.note: INFOSTEALER LOGS — the highest-value bucket in IntelX. One hit = one infected machine at one moment, with the URL/user/password triple and its session context. Read it per ITEM, not as a corpus: check whether the machine is a VICTIM of this campaign (credentials for the scam's own front-end) or the OPERATOR's own box (the panel URL, the CMS/registrar/exchange logins behind the campaign) — the second is direct attribution. Also the strictest handling: real victim credentials, so quote metadata and never paste secrets into a case file

pastes.note: pastebin-class documents — operators publish their own advertising, panels and configs here, so a hit is often the operator's OWN text

whois.note: historical WHOIS snapshots — an independent second source for a registrant selector when WhoisXML history is unavailable

darknet.tor.note: onion mirrors — market/forum listings naming the selector

leaks.private.general.note: non-public breach corpora — better provenance than the public ones, still a user table: a date and an exposure fact, not a link

web.public.note: IntelX's own crawl, split per TLD as web.public.<tld> — a snapshot of the page as IntelX saw it, useful when the site is dead and Wayback missed it

leaks.public.general.note: public breach corpora — the LOWEST-yield 'leak' hit. Presence dates the address's exposure and nothing more; these dumps are recycled across dozens of combolists, so the same address reappears for years with no new information

dumpster.note: unsorted intake — treat every hit as unverified

search_plan._comment: HOW A SELECTOR IS SEARCHED — the order of the passes and the order of the selectors. Two decisions live here, and both exist because IntelX returns a BOUNDED page: what you ask for first is what you actually get. (1) LOGS FIRST. A general search on a long-exposed address comes back overwhelmingly recycled combolist rows; `max_records` fills with them and the one infostealer-log entry that would have made the case is truncated away before the analyst ever sees it — sorting the page afterwards cannot recover a record that was never returned. So an unscoped search runs as TWO passes: a bucket-scoped pass over `first_pass_buckets` (the stealer logs), then the general pass for everything else. Each pass costs its own unit, which is the price of not letting the public breach corpora crowd out the logs; when the budget only allows one, the logs pass is the one that runs. Set `general_pass` false on a tight allowance to buy logs coverage on twice as many selectors. An explicit `--buckets` from the analyst always overrides the plan. (2) SELECTOR PRIORITY. When a bounded allowance is spread across a result's artifacts, this is the order they are spent in. DOMAIN AND EMAIL LEAD, and the domain is first on purpose: a stealer-log record is indexed by the URL it captured, so searching the CASE DOMAIN returns the machines that held credentials FOR that domain — the campaign's victims and, when the operator logged into their own panel from an infected box, the operator's machine. That is the single highest-yield IntelX move on a web case, and no other layer in this toolkit can reach it. The email is next because it is the selector that carries identity across corpora.

media_types._comment: The `media` code on each record — what KIND of document matched. Used to label results and to filter a search (media=0 means all). Codes 10-12 are reserved by IntelX and must not be sent.

phonebook_targets._comment: The `target` value for a PHONEBOOK search — the endpoint that turns ONE domain into an inventory of the selectors IntelX has seen under it. This is the highest-value call in the whole layer for web casework: point it at an apex and it returns the email addresses, the subdomains and the URLs, which are exactly the artifacts the rest of WebPivot pivots on. It is a PAID endpoint (see plan_capabilities) — a free key gets the web UI instead.

selector_result_types._comment: The `selectortype` code on each phonebook/selector result, so output can be grouped by artifact class rather than dumped as one list.

plan_capabilities._comment: What each IntelX entitlement can do, so the tool degrades with an accurate sentence instead of an opaque HTTP error. `phonebook` is the one that matters most: it is PAID-ONLY, so on a free key the domain->emails/subdomains inventory must be reported as NOT RUN rather than as empty. `file_read` gates reading a leak item's actual content (metadata is still returned without it).

none.note: no key — the query BUILDER and the web-UI links still work; nothing is queried from here

free.note: free/public key: metadata search over the public buckets; phonebook and item content are refused (HTTP 402/403)

api.note: paid API key: search + phonebook + item content, metered in credits

enterprise.note: as api, with the private buckets and higher limits

search_budget._comment: THE SPEND GUARD. IntelX meters searches (a free key gets a small daily allowance; a paid key spends credits), and — unlike a rate limit — running out is silent from the analyst's side: the search simply returns nothing and an empty result reads as 'the operator is not in any leak'. So spend is counted from MEMORY/api_usage.jsonl before the call and capped per run and per month, exactly like the Censys guard. `phonebook_costs` reflects that a phonebook search is the expensive call and should not be fired at every domain in a 200-host batch. Override per run with INTELX_MAX_SEARCHES_PER_RUN / INTELX_MONTHLY_SEARCHES.

result_limits._comment: Per-call ceilings the tool applies so one selector cannot dominate a case file or a poll loop. `max_records` is what is kept from a search, `poll_*` bound the two-step result fetch, and `preview_lines` is how much of an item's content is pulled when previewing.

ui_templates._comment: The KEYLESS deliverable. Every IntelX pivot emits these URLs so an analyst with only a free web account can run the identical selector by hand — the same degradation path as the Censys CenQL builder. `{term}` is URL-encoded by the caller.

clustering_policy._comment: FALSE-POSITIVE CONTROL — read this before turning an IntelX hit into a same-operator edge. IntelX answers 'where has this selector been seen', which is a question about EXPOSURE, not about ownership. Co-membership in a corpus is the textbook false cluster: two addresses in the same combolist share a victim population, not an operator, so `never_cluster_on` is about the CORPUS, not about the value of its items. STEALER LOGS ARE THE ONE PLACE THAT DISTINCTION BITES: `leaks.logs` is listed here because 'both selectors appear in the log corpus' proves nothing (millions of machines), but a SINGLE log item can be first-class attribution — if that machine holds the campaign's panel URL and credentials, the operator's own box is in the dump, and that is per-ITEM evidence read by hand, not an automatic edge. See `item_evidence` below. Everything in `cluster_on` may support an edge, and even there the rule is the repo's usual one: corroborate with a second, independent artifact class before committing it.
clustering_policy.note: Corpus co-membership is never a link. But a stealer-log ITEM is worth opening: read whether the infected machine is a VICTIM of this campaign (holds credentials for the scam's front-end) or the OPERATOR (holds the admin panel, the registrar/CMS/exchange logins behind it). The second is attribution; the first feeds the victim/access-vector layer. A breach-dump item is worth opening for its DATE and nothing else.
